summary: Deuteronomy 31 (30 verses) continues the story of covenant renewal. Starting with 'Moses went and spoke these words to all Israel.', it moves through themes of covenant renewal, obedience and calls readers toward love.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows covenant renewal lived out in plains of moab. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

context.author: Moses

questions.question: What is happening in Deuteronomy 31?
questions.answer: In 30 verses, this chapter deuteronomy 31 (30 verses) continues the story of covenant renewal. starting with 'moses went and spoke these words to all israel.', it moves through themes of covenant renewal, obedience and calls readers toward love. The setting is plains of moab, written to israel on edge of promised land. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Deuteronomy and why 31 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally moses, addressed to israel on edge of promised land around ~1400 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as farewell sermon — its themes of covenant renewal, obedience build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'covenant' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Binding promise/agreement God makes with people. In this chapter, it appears in context of covenant renewal. For a first-time reader: think of it as binding promise/agreement god makes with people, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through covenant renewal and obedience, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 21 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'It will happen, when many evils and troubles have come on them, that this song will testify before them as a witness; for it will not be forgotten out of the mouths of their descen...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about covenant renewal. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
